**Greta Garbo**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-1) (born **Greta Lovisa Gustafsson**;[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-2) 18 September 1905 – 15 April 1990) was a Swedish and American[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:1-3) film actress. She was a leading star during Hollywood's [silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") and early [golden eras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Hollywood_cinema "Classical Hollywood cinema"). Regarded as one of the greatest screen actresses of all time, she is known for her melancholic and somber screen persona, her film portrayals of [tragic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy "Tragedy") characters, and her subtle and understated performances. In 1999, the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") ranked Garbo fifth on its list of the [greatest female stars of classic Hollywood cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFI's_100_Years...100_Stars "AFI's 100 Years...100 Stars").

Garbo launched her career with a supporting role in the 1924 Swedish film _[The Saga of Gösta Berling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Saga\_of\_Gosta\_Berling "The Saga of Gosta Berling")_. Her performance caught the attention of [Louis B. Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_B._Mayer "Louis B. Mayer"), chief executive of [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer") (MGM), who brought her to Hollywood in 1925. She stirred interest with her first American silent film, _[Torrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrent\_(1926\_film) "Torrent (1926 film)")_ (1926). Garbo's performance in _[Flesh and the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flesh\_and\_the\_Devil "Flesh and the Devil")_ (1926), her third movie in the United States, made her an international star.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira200538-4) In 1928, Garbo starred in _[A Woman of Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Woman\_of\_Affairs "A Woman of Affairs"),_ which catapulted her to MGM's highest box-office star, surpassing the long-reigning [Lillian Gish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Gish "Lillian Gish"). Other well-known Garbo films from the silent era are _[The Mysterious Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mysterious\_Lady "The Mysterious Lady")_ (1928), _[The Single Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Single\_Standard "The Single Standard")_ (1929), and _[The Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kiss\_(1929\_film) "The Kiss (1929 film)")_ (1929).

With Garbo's first [sound film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_film "Sound film"), _[Anna Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Christie\_(1930\_English-language\_film) "Anna Christie (1930 English-language film)")_ (1930), MGM marketers enticed the public with the tagline "Garbo talks!" That same year she starred in _[Romance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance\_(1930\_film) "Romance (1930 film)")_ and for her performances in both films she received her first combined nomination out of three nominations for the [Academy Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-5) By 1932, her success allowed her to dictate the terms of her contracts and she became increasingly selective about her roles. She continued in films such as _[Mata Hari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mata\_Hari\_(1931\_film) "Mata Hari (1931 film)")_ (1931), _[Susan Lenox (Her Fall and Rise)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan\_Lenox\_(Her\_Fall\_and\_Rise) "Susan Lenox (Her Fall and Rise)")_ (1931), _[Grand Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Hotel\_(1932\_film) "Grand Hotel (1932 film)")_ (1932), _[Queen Christina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen\_Christina\_(film) "Queen Christina (film)")_ (1933), and _[Anna Karenina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Karenina\_(1935\_film) "Anna Karenina (1935 film)")_ (1935).

Many critics and film historians consider her performance as the doomed courtesan [Marguerite Gautier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lady_of_the_Camellias "The Lady of the Camellias") in _[Camille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille\_(1936\_film) "Camille (1936 film)")_ (1936) to be her finest and the role gained her a third Academy Award nomination. However, Garbo's career eventually declined and she became one of many stars labelled [box office poison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_Office_Poison_(magazine_article) "Box Office Poison (magazine article)") in 1938. Her career revived with a turn to comedy in _[Ninotchka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninotchka "Ninotchka")_ (1939), which earned her a fourth Academy Award nomination. _[Two-Faced Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-Faced\_Woman "Two-Faced Woman")_ (1941), which received poor reviews, was the last of her 28 feature films. Following this commercial failure, she continued to be offered movie roles, though she declined most of them. Those she did accept failed to materialize, either due to lack of funds or because she dropped out during filming. In 1954, Garbo was awarded an [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") "for her luminous and unforgettable screen performances".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-awardsdatabase.oscars.org-6)

Over time, Garbo would decline all opportunities to return to the screen. In her retirement, she shunned publicity, led a private life, and became an art collector whose paintings included works by [Pierre-Auguste Renoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Auguste_Renoir "Pierre-Auguste Renoir"), [Pierre Bonnard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bonnard "Pierre Bonnard") and [Kees van Dongen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kees_van_Dongen "Kees van Dongen").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-7) Although she refused throughout her life to talk to friends about her reasons for retiring, four years before her death, she told Swedish biographer Sven Broman: "I was tired of Hollywood. I did not like my work. There were many days when I had to force myself to go to the studio... I really wanted to live another life."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBroman1990271-8)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Greta_Lovisa_Gustafsson_-_Greta_Garbo_-_1905_-_1990_Zweeds_actrice%2C_SFA005001758.jpg/250px-Greta_Lovisa_Gustafsson_-_Greta_Garbo_-_1905_-_1990_Zweeds_actrice%2C_SFA005001758.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta_Lovisa_Gustafsson_-_Greta_Garbo_-_1905_-_1990_Zweeds_actrice,_SFA005001758.jpg)

Ten-year-old Garbo in 1915

Greta Lovisa Gustafsson[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-LCSN-19401104-9) was born in [Södermalm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%B6dermalm "Södermalm"), Stockholm, Sweden at 7:30 p.m.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Greta_Garbo:_A_Divine_Star-10) She was the third, and youngest, child of Anna Lovisa (née Karlsson, 1872–1944), who worked at a jam factory, and Karl Alfred Gustafsson (1871–1920), a laborer.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-WareBraukman2004p227-228-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Sjolander1971p12-13-12) She had an older brother, Sven Alfred (1898–1967), and an older sister, Alva Maria (1903–1926).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Furhammar1991p129-13) Garbo was nicknamed Kata, which was how she had mispronounced her first name, for the first ten years of her life.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Greta_Garbo:_A_Divine_Star-10)

Her parents met in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"), where her father had been visiting from [Frinnaryd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frinnaryd "Frinnaryd"). He moved to Stockholm to become independent and worked as a street cleaner, grocer, factory worker and butcher's assistant.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESouhami199464-14) He married Anna, who moved from [Högsby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B6gsby "Högsby").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBainbridge1955b76-16) The family was impoverished and lived in a three-bedroom cold-water flat at Blekingegatan No. 32. They raised their three children in a working-class district regarded as the city's slum.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-DAmico1962p901-17) Garbo later recalled:

> It was eternally grey—those long winter's nights. My father would be sitting in a corner, scribbling figures on a newspaper. On the other side of the room, my mother is repairing ragged old clothes, sighing. We children would be talking in very low voices, or just sitting silently. We were filled with anxiety, as if there were danger in the air. Such evenings are unforgettable for a sensitive girl, but also for a girl like me. Where we lived, all the houses and apartments looked alike, their ugliness matched by everything surrounding us.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Lektyr1931-18)

Garbo was a shy daydreamer as a child.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Corporation1974-19) She disliked school[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Biery1928a-hatesc-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-21) and preferred to play alone.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Biery1928a-noplay-22) She was a natural leader[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson199725-23) who became interested in theatre at an early age.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Biery1928a-sixorseven-24) She directed her friends in make-believe games and performances,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson199726-25) and dreamed of becoming an actress.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Biery1928a-sixorseven-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Biery1928a-dreaming-26) Later, she would participate in amateur theatre with her friends and frequent the [Mosebacke Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%B6dra_Teatern "Södra Teatern").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Lacouture1999-27) At the age of 13, Garbo graduated from school,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-28) and, typical of a Swedish working-class girl at that time, she did not attend high school. She later acknowledged a resulting [inferiority complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inferiority_complex "Inferiority complex").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson199732-29)

[![Image 7: Hand-written letter with multiple signatures and with stamps of approval.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Approved_application_for_Greta_Gustafsson_to_change_her_name_to_Greta_Garbo.jpg/250px-Approved_application_for_Greta_Gustafsson_to_change_her_name_to_Greta_Garbo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Approved_application_for_Greta_Gustafsson_to_change_her_name_to_Greta_Garbo.jpg)

The approved application by Greta's mother to allow her name change from Gustafsson to Garbo.

The [Spanish flu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1918_flu_pandemic "1918 flu pandemic") spread throughout Stockholm in the winter of 1919 and her father, to whom she was very close, became ill and lost his job.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Parish2007-30) Garbo cared for him, taking him to the hospital for weekly treatments. He died in 1920 when she was 14 years old.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBainbridge1955b76-16)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTENYTimes1990-31)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1920–1924: Beginnings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1920–1924: Beginnings")]

Garbo first worked as a soap-lather girl in a barber shop before taking a job in the [PUB department store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PUB_(Stockholm) "PUB (Stockholm)") where she ran errands and worked in the [millinery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millinery "Millinery") department. After modeling hats for the store's catalogues, Garbo earned a more lucrative job as a fashion model at [Nordiska Kompaniet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordiska_Kompaniet "Nordiska Kompaniet").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson199736-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-33) In 1920, a director of film commercials for the store cast Garbo in roles advertising women's clothing. Her first commercial premiered on 12 December 1920.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Herr-34) In 1922, Garbo caught the attention of director [Erik A. Petschler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_A._Petschler "Erik A. Petschler"), who gave her a part, credited as Greta Gustafson, in his short comedy _Peter the Tramp_, released as _Luffar-Petter_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-SFdb/3537-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-nypl/Luffar-Petter_|-36)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis199434-37)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-loc.gov/2021670583-38)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Greta_Garbo_in_G%C3%B6sta_Berlings_Saga_1924_cropped.jpg/330px-Greta_Garbo_in_G%C3%B6sta_Berlings_Saga_1924_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta_Garbo_in_G%C3%B6sta_Berlings_Saga_1924_cropped.jpg)

Garbo in her first leading role in the Swedish film [_The Saga of Gösta Berling_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Saga_of_Gosta_Berling "The Saga of Gosta Berling") (1924) with [Lars Hanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lars_Hanson "Lars Hanson")

From 1922 to 1924, she studied at the [Royal Dramatic Training Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Dramatic_Training_Academy "Royal Dramatic Training Academy") in Stockholm. She was recruited in 1924 by the Finnish director [Mauritz Stiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritz_Stiller "Mauritz Stiller") to play a principal part in his film _[The Saga of Gösta Berling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Saga\_of\_Gosta\_Berling "The Saga of Gosta Berling")_, a dramatization of the [famous novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6sta_Berlings_Saga "Gösta Berlings Saga") by [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_for_Literature "Nobel Prize for Literature") winner [Selma Lagerlöf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selma_Lagerl%C3%B6f "Selma Lagerlöf"), which also featured the actor [Lars Hanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lars_Hanson "Lars Hanson"). Stiller became her mentor, training her as a film actress and managing all aspects of her nascent career.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis199454%E2%80%9361-39) She followed her role in _Gösta Berling_ with a starring role in the German film _[Die freudlose Gasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die\_freudlose\_Gasse "Die freudlose Gasse")_ (_Joyless Street_ or _The Street of Sorrow_, 1925), directed by [G. W. Pabst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G._W._Pabst "G. W. Pabst") and co-starring [Asta Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asta_Nielsen "Asta Nielsen").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis199467%E2%80%9369-40) She praised Asta and said: "In terms of expression and versatility, I am nothing to her."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-41)

Accounts differ on the circumstances of her first contract with [Louis B. Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_B._Mayer "Louis B. Mayer"), at that time vice president and general manager of [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer"). [Victor Seastrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Sj%C3%B6str%C3%B6m "Victor Sjöström"), a respected Swedish director at MGM, was a friend of Stiller and encouraged Mayer to meet him on a trip to Berlin. There are two recent versions of what happened next. In one,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson199772%E2%80%9374-42) Mayer, always looking for new talent, had done his research and was interested in Stiller. He made an offer, but Stiller demanded that Garbo be part of any contract, convinced that she would be an asset to his career. Mayer balked, but eventually agreed to a private viewing of _Gösta Berling_. He was immediately struck by Garbo's magnetism and became more interested in her than in Stiller. "It was her eyes," his daughter recalled him saying, "I can make a star out of her." In the second version,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis199480%E2%80%9383-43) Mayer had already seen _Gösta Berling_ before his Berlin trip, and Garbo, not Stiller, was his primary interest. On the way to the screening, Mayer said to his daughter: "This director is wonderful, but what we really ought to look at is the girl... The girl, look at the girl!" After the screening, his daughter reported, he was unwavering: "I'll take her without him. I'll take her _with_ him. Number one is the girl."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira20059-44)

### 1925–1929: Silent film stardom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1925–1929: Silent film stardom")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Portrait_photograph_of_Greta_Garbo%2C_1925.jpg/250px-Portrait_photograph_of_Greta_Garbo%2C_1925.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_photograph_of_Greta_Garbo,_1925.jpg)

Portrait photograph of Greta Garbo, 1925

In 1925, Garbo, who was unable to speak English, was brought to Hollywood from Sweden at the request of Mayer. After a 10-day crossing on the [_Drottningholm_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Virginian#Drottningholm "RMS Virginian")[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-45) in July, Garbo and Stiller arrived in New York where they remained for more than six months without word from MGM. They decided to travel to Los Angeles on their own but another five weeks passed without contact from the studio.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis199484-46)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson199785-47) On the verge of returning to Sweden, Garbo wrote her boyfriend back home, "You're quite right when you think I don't feel at home here... Oh, you lovely little Sweden, I promise that when I return to you, my sad face will smile as never before."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Sands-48) A Swedish friend in Los Angeles helped by contacting MGM production boss [Irving Thalberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Thalberg "Irving Thalberg"), who agreed to give Garbo a screen test. According to author Frederick Sands, "the result of the test was electrifying. Thalberg was impressed and began grooming the young actress the following day, arranging to fix her teeth, making sure she lost weight and giving her English lessons."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Sands-48)

During her rise to stardom, film historian Mark Vieira notes, "Thalberg decreed that henceforth, Garbo would play a young, but worldly wise, woman."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Vieira-1-49) However, according to Thalberg's actress wife, [Norma Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Shearer "Norma Shearer"), Garbo did not necessarily agree with his ideas stating "Miss Garbo at first didn't like playing the exotic, the sophisticated, the woman of the world. She used to complain, "Mr. Thalberg, I am just a young gur-rl!" Irving tossed it off with a laugh. With those elegant pictures, he was creating the Garbo image".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Vieira-1-49) Although she expected to work with Stiller on her first film,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Wollstein1994-50) she was cast in _[Torrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrent\_(1926\_film) "Torrent (1926 film)")_ (1926), an adaptation of a novel by [Vicente Blasco Ibáñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Blasco_Ib%C3%A1%C3%B1ez "Vicente Blasco Ibáñez"), with director [Monta Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monta_Bell "Monta Bell"). She replaced [Aileen Pringle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aileen_Pringle "Aileen Pringle"), 10 years her senior, and played a peasant girl turned singer, opposite [Ricardo Cortez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Cortez "Ricardo Cortez").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Katchmer1991-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-WalkerMetro-Goldwyn-Mayer1980-52)_Torrent_ was a hit, and, despite its cool reception by the trade press,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Jacobs2008-53) Garbo's performance was well received.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Variety-Torrent-54)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-HallHadaunt1926-55)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Flesh_and_the_Devil_with_John_Gilbert.jpg/330px-Flesh_and_the_Devil_with_John_Gilbert.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flesh_and_the_Devil_with_John_Gilbert.jpg)

Garbo in _[Flesh and the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flesh\_and\_the\_Devil "Flesh and the Devil")_ (1926) with [John Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gilbert_(actor) "John Gilbert (actor)")

Garbo's success in her first American film led Thalberg to cast her in a similar role in _[The Temptress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Temptress\_(1926\_film) "The Temptress (1926 film)")_ (1926), based on another Ibáñez novel. In this, her second film, she played opposite the popular star [Antonio Moreno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Moreno "Antonio Moreno")[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Resto2008-56) but was given top billing. Her mentor Stiller, who had persuaded her to take the part, was assigned to direct.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Thomsen1997p129-57) For both Garbo (who did not want to play another vamp and did not like the script any more than she did the first one)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Flamini1994-58) and Stiller, _The Temptress_ was a harrowing experience. Stiller, who spoke little English, had difficulty adapting to the studio system[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Biery1928c-Stiller-artist-59) and did not get on with Moreno,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Golden2001-60) was fired by Thalberg and replaced by [Fred Niblo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Niblo "Fred Niblo"). Re-shooting _The Temptress_ was expensive, and even though it became one of the top-grossing films of the 1926–1927 season,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira200967-61) it was the only Garbo film of the period to lose money.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Koszarski1994-62) However, Garbo received rave reviews,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Brown1965-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-ConwayMcGregorRicci1968p51-64)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Zierold1969p164-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-HallMorduant1926-66) and MGM had a new star.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira200967-61)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994108-67)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Garbo_-_Gilbert_-_publicity.jpg/250px-Garbo_-_Gilbert_-_publicity.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Garbo_-_Gilbert_-_publicity.jpg)

Garbo with [John Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gilbert_(actor) "John Gilbert (actor)") in _[A Woman of Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Woman\_of\_Affairs "A Woman of Affairs")_ (1928)

After her lightning ascent, Garbo made eight more silent films, and all were hits.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994568%E2%80%93570-68) She starred in three of them with the leading man [John Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gilbert_(actor) "John Gilbert (actor)").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994124%E2%80%93125-69) About their first movie, _[Flesh and the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flesh\_and\_the\_Devil "Flesh and the Devil")_ (1926), silent film expert [Kevin Brownlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Brownlow "Kevin Brownlow") states that "she gave a more erotic performance than Hollywood had ever seen."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-TCMBrownlow-70) Their on-screen chemistry soon translated into an off-camera romance, and by the end of the production, they began living together.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994121-71) The film also marked a turning point in Garbo's career. Vieira wrote: "Audiences were mesmerized by her beauty and titillated by her love scenes with Gilbert. She was a sensation."[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira200969-72) Profits from her third movie with Gilbert, _[A Woman of Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Woman\_of\_Affairs "A Woman of Affairs")_ (1928), catapulted her to top Metro star of the 1928–1929 box office season, usurping the long-reigned silent queen [Lillian Gish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Gish "Lillian Gish").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997193-73) In 1929, reviewer Pierre de Rohan wrote in the _New York Telegraph_: "She has glamour and fascination for both sexes which have never been equaled on the screen."[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997220-74)

The impact of Garbo's acting and screen presence quickly established her reputation as one of Hollywood's greatest actresses. Film historian and critic [David Denby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Denby "David Denby") argues that Garbo introduced a subtlety of expression to the art of silent acting and that its effect on audiences cannot be exaggerated. She "lowers her head to look calculating or flutters her lips," he says. "Her face darkens with a slight tightening around the eyes and mouth; she registers a passing idea with a contraction of her brows or a drooping of her lids. Worlds turned on her movements."[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-75)

During this period, Garbo began to require unusual conditions during the shooting of her scenes. She prohibited visitors—including the studio brass—from her sets and demanded that black flats or screens surround her to prevent extras and technicians from watching her. When asked about these eccentric requirements, she said: "If I am by myself, my face will do things I cannot do with it otherwise."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994301%E2%80%93320-76)

Despite her status as a star of silent films,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrafton1999495%E2%80%93496-77) the studio feared that her Swedish accent might impair her work in sound, and delayed the shift for as long as possible.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrafton1999295-78)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Limbacher1968p219-79) MGM itself was the last Hollywood studio to convert to sound,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrafton1999206%E2%80%93207-80) and Garbo's last silent film, _[The Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Kiss\_(1929\_film) "The Kiss (1929 film)")_ (1929), was also the studio's.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005100-81) Despite the fears, Garbo became one of the biggest box-office draws of the next decade.

### 1930–1939: Transition to sound and continued success

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1930–1939: Transition to sound and continued success")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Greta_Garbo_in_a_publicity_image_for_%22Anna_Christie%22.jpg/250px-Greta_Garbo_in_a_publicity_image_for_%22Anna_Christie%22.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta_Garbo_in_a_publicity_image_for_%22Anna_Christie%22.jpg)

Garbo in her first sound film _[Anna Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Christie\_(1930\_English-language\_film) "Anna Christie (1930 English-language film)")_ (1930).

In late 1929, MGM cast Garbo in _[Anna Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Christie\_(1930\_English-language\_film) "Anna Christie (1930 English-language film)")_ (1930), a film adaptation of the [1922 play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Christie "Anna Christie") by [Eugene O'Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_O'Neill "Eugene O'Neill"), her first speaking role. The screenplay was adapted by [Frances Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Marion "Frances Marion"), and the film was produced by [Irving Thalberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Thalberg "Irving Thalberg") and [Paul Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bern "Paul Bern"). Sixteen minutes into the film, she famously utters her first line, "Gimme a whiskey, ginger ale on the side, and don't be stingy, baby." The film premiered in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") on 21 February 1930, publicized with the catchphrase "Garbo talks!", and was the highest-grossing film of the year.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005111-82) Her performance received positive reviews; [Mordaunt Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mordaunt_Hall "Mordaunt Hall") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ remarked that Garbo was "even more interesting through being heard than she was in her mute portrayals. She reveals no nervousness before the microphone and her careful interpretation of Anna can scarcely be disputed."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-hall-83) Garbo received her first [Academy Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress") nomination for her performance, although she lost to MGM colleague [Norma Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Shearer "Norma Shearer"). Her nomination that year included her performance in _[Romance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance\_(1930\_film) "Romance (1930 film)")_ (1930). After filming ended, Garbo—along with a different director and cast—filmed a [German-language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") version of _[Anna Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Christie\_(1930\_German-language\_film) "Anna Christie (1930 German-language film)")_ that was released in December 1930.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994570-84) The film's success certified Garbo's successful transition to [talkies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_film "Sound film"). In her follow-up film, _Romance_, she portrayed an [Italian opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_opera "Italian opera") star, opposite [Lewis Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Stone "Lewis Stone"). She was paired opposite [Robert Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Montgomery_(actor) "Robert Montgomery (actor)") in _[Inspiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspiration\_(1931\_film) "Inspiration (1931 film)")_ (1931), and her profile was used to boost the career of the relatively unknown [Clark Gable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Gable "Clark Gable") in _[Susan Lenox (Her Fall and Rise)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan\_Lenox\_(Her\_Fall\_and\_Rise) "Susan Lenox (Her Fall and Rise)")_ (1931). Although the films did not match Garbo's success with her sound debut, she was ranked as the most popular female star in the United States in 1930 and 1931.

Garbo followed with two of her best-remembered roles. She played the [World War I German spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mata_Hari "Mata Hari") in the lavish production of _[Mata Hari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mata\_Hari\_(1931\_film) "Mata Hari (1931 film)")_ (1931), opposite [Ramón Novarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ram%C3%B3n_Novarro "Ramón Novarro"). When the film was released, it "caused panic, with police reserves required to keep the waiting mob in order."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-85) The following year, she played a [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") ballerina in _[Grand Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Hotel\_(1932\_film) "Grand Hotel (1932 film)")_ (1932), opposite an ensemble cast, including [John Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Barrymore "John Barrymore"), [Joan Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Crawford "Joan Crawford"), and [Wallace Beery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Beery "Wallace Beery"), among others. The film won that year's [Academy Award for Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture"). Both films were MGM's highest-earning films of 1931 and 1932, respectively, and Garbo was dubbed "the greatest money-making machine ever put on screen".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTENYTimes1990-31)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997244-86)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994284-87) Garbo's close friend [Mercedes de Acosta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_de_Acosta "Mercedes de Acosta") then penned a screenplay for her to portray [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc "Joan of Arc"),[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994269%E2%80%93270-88) but MGM rebuffed the idea, and the project was shelved. By this time she had a fanatical worldwide following and the phenomenon of "Garbomania" reached its peak.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-89) After appearing in _[As You Desire Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/As\_You\_Desire\_Me\_(film) "As You Desire Me (film)")_ (1932), the first of three films in which Garbo starred opposite [Melvyn Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvyn_Douglas "Melvyn Douglas"), her MGM contract expired, and she returned to Sweden.

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/8d/Greta_Garbo_-_1936.jpg/250px-Greta_Garbo_-_1936.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta_Garbo_-_1936.jpg)

In _Camille_ (1936)

After nearly a year of negotiations, Garbo agreed to renew her contract with MGM on the condition that she would star in _[Queen Christina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen\_Christina\_(film) "Queen Christina (film)")_ (1933), and her salary would be increased to $300,000 per film. The film's screenplay had been written by [Salka Viertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salka_Viertel "Salka Viertel"); although reluctant to make the movie, MGM relented at Garbo's insistence. For her leading man, MGM suggested [Charles Boyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Boyer "Charles Boyer") or [Laurence Olivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier "Laurence Olivier"), but Garbo rejected both, preferring her former co-star and lover [John Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gilbert_(actor) "John Gilbert (actor)"). The studio balked at the idea of casting Gilbert, fearing his declining career would hurt the film's box-office, but Garbo prevailed.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005183-90)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005181-91)_Queen Christina_ was a lavish production, becoming one of the studio's biggest productions at the time. Publicized as "Garbo returns", the film premiered in December 1933 to positive reviews and box-office triumph and became the highest-grossing film of the year. The movie, however, met with controversy upon its release; censors objected to the scenes in which Garbo disguised herself as a man and kissed a female co-star.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994572%E2%80%93573-92)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997316-93)

Although her domestic popularity was undiminished in the early 1930s, high profits for Garbo's films after _Queen Christina_ depended on the foreign market for their success.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994572%E2%80%93573-92)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997316-93) The type of historical and melodramatic films she began to make on the advice of Viertel were highly successful abroad, but considerably less so in the United States. In the midst of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States "Great Depression in the United States"), American screen audiences seemed to favor "home-grown" screen couples, such as [Clark Gable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Gable "Clark Gable") and [Jean Harlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Harlow "Jean Harlow"). [David O. Selznick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_O._Selznick "David O. Selznick") wanted to cast Garbo as the dying heiress in _[Dark Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark\_Victory "Dark Victory")_ (eventually released in 1939 with other leads), but she chose [Leo Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy "Leo Tolstoy")'s _[Anna Karenina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna\_Karenina\_(1935\_film) "Anna Karenina (1935 film)")_ (1935), in which she played another of her renowned roles.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005207%E2%80%93210-94) Her performance won her the [New York Film Critics Circle Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Film_Critics_Circle_Award_for_Best_Actress "New York Film Critics Circle Award for Best Actress"). The film was successful in international markets, and had better domestic rentals than MGM anticipated.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994172,_571-95) Still, its profit was significantly diminished because of Garbo's exorbitant salary.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005216-96)

Garbo selected [George Cukor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Cukor "George Cukor")'s romantic drama _[Camille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille\_(1936\_film) "Camille (1936 film)")_ (1936) as her next project. Thalberg cast her opposite [Robert Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Taylor_(American_actor) "Robert Taylor (American actor)") and former co-star, [Lionel Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Barrymore "Lionel Barrymore"). Cukor carefully crafted Garbo's portrayal of Marguerite Gautier, a lower-class woman, who becomes the world-renowned mistress Camille. Production was marred, however, by the sudden death of Thalberg, then only thirty-seven, which plunged the Hollywood studios into a "state of profound shock", writes [David Bret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bret "David Bret").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Bret-97):272 Garbo had grown close to Thalberg and his wife, [Norma Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Shearer "Norma Shearer"), and had often dropped by their house unannounced. Her grief for Thalberg, some believe, was more profound than for [John Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gilbert_(actor) "John Gilbert (actor)"), who died earlier that same year.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Bret-97):272 His death also added to the sombre mood required for the closing scenes of _Camille_. When the film premiered in New York on 12 December 1936, it became an international success, Garbo's first major success in three years. She won the [New York Film Critics Circle Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Film_Critics_Circle_Award_for_Best_Actress "New York Film Critics Circle Award for Best Actress") for her performance, and she was nominated once more for an Academy Award. Garbo regarded _Camille_ as her favorite out of all of her films.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-98)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Modern_Screen_1937_Conquest.jpg/250px-Modern_Screen_1937_Conquest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Modern_Screen_1937_Conquest.jpg)

Garbo and [Charles Boyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Boyer "Charles Boyer") in _[Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest\_(1937\_film) "Conquest (1937 film)")_ (1937)

Garbo's follow-up project was [Clarence Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Brown "Clarence Brown")'s lavish production of _[Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest\_(1937\_film) "Conquest (1937 film)")_ (1937), opposite [Charles Boyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Boyer "Charles Boyer"). The plot was the dramatized romance between [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon") and [Marie Walewska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Walewska "Marie Walewska"). It was MGM's biggest and most-publicized movie of its year, but upon its release, it became one of the studio's biggest failures of the decade at the box office.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997316-93) When her contract expired soon thereafter, she returned briefly to Sweden. On 3 May 1938, Garbo was among the many stars—including [Joan Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Crawford "Joan Crawford"), [Norma Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norma_Shearer "Norma Shearer"), [Luise Rainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luise_Rainer "Luise Rainer"), [Katharine Hepburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katharine_Hepburn "Katharine Hepburn"), [Mae West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mae_West "Mae West"), [Marlene Dietrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dietrich "Marlene Dietrich"), [Fred Astaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Astaire "Fred Astaire"), and [Dolores del Río](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolores_del_R%C3%ADo "Dolores del Río"), among others—dubbed to be "[Box Office Poison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_Office_Poison_(magazine_article) "Box Office Poison (magazine article)")" in an article published by Harry Brandt on behalf of the Independent Theatre Owners of America.

After the box-office failure of _Conquest_, MGM decided a change of pace was needed to resurrect Garbo's career. For her next movie, the studio teamed her with producer-director [Ernst Lubitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Lubitsch "Ernst Lubitsch") to film _[Ninotchka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninotchka "Ninotchka")_ (1939), her first comedy. The film was one of the first Hollywood movies which, under the cover of a satirical, light romance, depicted the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") under [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin") as being rigid and gray when compared to Paris in its pre-war years. _Ninotchka_ premiered in October 1939, publicized with the catchphrase "Garbo laughs!", commenting on the departure of Garbo's serious and melancholy image as she transferred to comedy. Favoured by critics and box-office success in the United States and abroad, it was banned in the Soviet Union.

### 1941–1948: Last work and retirement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1941–1948: Last work and retirement")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Twofaced_woman.jpg/330px-Twofaced_woman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Twofaced_woman.jpg)

Garbo and [Melvyn Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvyn_Douglas "Melvyn Douglas") in _[Two-Faced Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-Faced\_Woman "Two-Faced Woman")_ (1941)

With George Cukor's _[Two-Faced Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-Faced\_Woman "Two-Faced Woman")_ (1941), MGM attempted to capitalize on Garbo's success in _Ninotchka_ by re-teaming her with Melvyn Douglas in another romantic comedy which sought to transform her into a chic, modern woman. She played a "double" role that featured her dancing the [rhumba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhumba "Rhumba"), swimming, and skiing. The film was a critical failure, but, contrary to popular belief, it performed reasonably well at the box office.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994573-99) Garbo referred to the film as "my grave".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBainbridge1955c129-100)_Two-Faced Woman_ was her last film; she was thirty-six and had made 28 feature films in a span of 16 years.

Although Garbo felt humiliated by the negative reviews of _Two-Faced Woman_, she did not intend to retire at first.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994381-101) But her films depended on the European market, and when it fell through because of the war, finding a vehicle was problematic for MGM.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005268-102)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994281-103) Garbo signed a one-picture deal in 1942 to make _The Girl from Leningrad_, but the project quickly dissolved.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005268-102) She still thought she would continue when the war was over,[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005268-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994383-104) though she was ambivalent and indecisive about returning to the screen. [Salka Viertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salka_Viertel "Salka Viertel"), Garbo's close friend and collaborator, said in 1945: "Greta is impatient to work. But on the other side, she's afraid of it."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005270-105) Garbo also worried about her age. "Time leaves traces on our small faces and bodies. It's not the same anymore, being able to pull it off."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005270-105) George Cukor, director of _Two-Faced Woman_, and often blamed for its failure, said: "People often glibly say that the failure of _Two-Faced Woman_ finished Garbo's career. That's a grotesque over-simplification. It certainly threw her, but I think that what really happened was that she just gave up. She didn't want to go on."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994383-104)

Still, Garbo signed a contract in 1948 with producer [Walter Wanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Wanger "Walter Wanger"), who had produced _Queen Christina_, to shoot a picture based on [Balzac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor%C3%A9_de_Balzac "Honoré de Balzac")'s _[La Duchesse de Langeais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Duchesse\_de\_Langeais "La Duchesse de Langeais")_. [Max Ophüls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Oph%C3%BCls "Max Ophüls") was slated to adapt and direct.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Reid2006p44-106)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Kellow2004p338-107)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-ForrestKoos2002p151-152-108) She made several [screen tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_test "Screen test"), learned the script, and arrived in Rome in the summer of 1949 to shoot the picture. However, the financing failed to materialize, and the project was abandoned.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBainbridge1955c130-109) The screen tests—the last time Garbo stepped in front of a movie camera—were thought to have been lost for 41 years until they were re-discovered in 1990 by film historians [Leonard Maltin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Maltin "Leonard Maltin") and [Jeanine Basinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanine_Basinger "Jeanine Basinger").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994426-110) Parts of the footage were included in the 2005 [TCM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_Classic_Movies "Turner Classic Movies") documentary _Garbo_.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-TCM-GarboDoc-111)

In 1949, she was offered the role of fictional silent-film star Norma Desmond in _[Sunset Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset\_Boulevard\_(film) "Sunset Boulevard (film)")_, directed by _Ninotchka_ co-writer [Billy Wilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Wilder "Billy Wilder"). However, after a meeting with film producer [Charles Brackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Brackett "Charles Brackett"), she insisted that she had no interest in the part whatsoever.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-112)

She was offered many roles in the 1940s as well as throughout her retirement years but rejected all but a few of them. In the few instances when she did accept them, the slightest problem led her to drop out.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira2005271-113) Although she refused throughout her life to talk to friends about her reasons for retiring, four years before her death, she told Swedish biographer Sven Broman: "I was tired of Hollywood. I did not like my work. There were many days when I had to force myself to go to the studio... I really wanted to live another life."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBroman1990271-8)

## Public persona

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Public persona")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Greta_Garbo_Grand_Hotel.jpg/250px-Greta_Garbo_Grand_Hotel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta_Garbo_Grand_Hotel.jpg)

Garbo in [_Grand Hotel_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Hotel_(1932_film) "Grand Hotel (1932 film)") (1932), in which she said the famous line "I want to be alone." The public would long associate her with these words due to her private lifestyle.

From the early days of her career, Garbo avoided industry social functions, preferring to spend her time alone or with friends. She never signed autographs or answered fan mail, and rarely gave interviews.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBainbridge1955a12-114)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-NYT-GarboBack-smokinglounge-115) Nor did she ever appear at Oscar ceremonies, even when she was nominated.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrutzen199246-116) Her aversion to publicity and the press was undeniably genuine,[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994129,_156%E2%80%93157,_243-117)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997196-118) and exasperating to the studio at first. In an interview in 1928, she explained that her desire for privacy began when she was a child, stating, "As early as I can remember, I have wanted to be alone. I've always been moody. I detest crowds, I don't like many people."[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-119)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:0-120) The artist [James Montgomery Flagg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Montgomery_Flagg "James Montgomery Flagg") said in 1933[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert193516,_19-121) that when he was allowed to sketch Garbo at a director's party in Hollywood some years earlier she told him she suffered from melancholia. At that time she had a Swedish phonograph record of laughs of all kinds which she played when visiting, to observe her hosts' response.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson2007150%E2%80%93151-122) In 1937, in a letter to her friend, Austrian actress and writer [Salka Viertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salka_Viertel "Salka Viertel"), she wrote: "I go nowhere, see no one... It is hard and sad to be alone, but sometimes it's even more difficult to be with someone..."[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-123) In another letter in 1970 she wrote: "I feel very tired and cannot seem to get myself together to plan where to go... I am sorry but something always seem to go a little wrong with me, and it is not in my head either..."[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-124)

Because Garbo was suspicious and mistrustful of the media, and often at odds with MGM executives, she spurned Hollywood's publicity rules. She was routinely referred to by the press as the "Swedish Sphinx". Her reticence and fear of strangers perpetuated the mystery and mystique she projected both on screen and in real life. MGM eventually capitalized on it, for it bolstered the image of the silent and reclusive woman of mystery.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994179-125)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrutzen199246-116)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997196%E2%80%93197-126) In spite of her strenuous efforts to avoid publicity, Garbo paradoxically became one of the twentieth century's most publicized women.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTENYTimes1990-31)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes1990-127) She is closely associated with a line from _Grand Hotel_, one which the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") in 2005 voted the [30th-most memorable movie quote of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFI's_100_Years...100_Movie_Quotes "AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes"),[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-128) "I want to be alone; I just want to be alone." The theme was a running gag in her movies that began during the silent period.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-NYT-Obit-let-alone-129)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-131) According to a 1955 piece in [LIFE magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_(magazine) "Life (magazine)"), Garbo explained that she'd said: "I want to be _let_ alone", not "I want to be alone".[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-132)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-133)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-134)

### Fashion and personal style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Fashion and personal style")]

After starring in _[Torrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrent\_(1926\_film) "Torrent (1926 film)")_ (1926), she became known as "the [Art Deco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Deco "Art Deco")[Diva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diva "Diva")".[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:0-120) She favored men's shoes and clothes[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:3-135) and her style has been described as "trench coat, simple shoes, shirts, [cigarette pants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slim-fit_pants "Slim-fit pants"), [slouch hat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slouch_hat "Slouch hat") and big sunglasses."[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:0-120) Garbo has been credited with popularizing the "slouchy hat".[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-136)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

### Retirement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Retirement")]

In her retirement, Garbo generally led a private life of simplicity and leisure. She made no public appearances and assiduously avoided the publicity she loathed.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis19945,_57,_156%E2%80%93158_passim-137) Contrary to myth, from the beginning she had many friends and acquaintances with whom she socialized and travelled,[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997244,_508%E2%80%93509_passim-138)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994-139) although it has also been said that in later years she did not trust many people and therefore did not have many close friends. Her usual response to anyone asking her about a comeback was "I have made enough faces", as she once said to [David Niven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Niven "David Niven").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:2-140)

Garbo was often perplexed about what to do and how to spend her time, always struggling with her many eccentricities[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994-139)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997-141) and her life-long melancholy and moodiness.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis19948%E2%80%939,_107%E2%80%93108,_167,_329%E2%80%93330,_506%E2%80%93511_passim-142)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson199787,_91,_115,_143_passim-143) ("Drifting" was the word she frequently used; in 1946 she told reporters, "I have no plans, either for the movies or anything else. I'm just drifting."[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994417,_445-144)) As she approached her sixtieth birthday in 1965, she told a frequent walking companion, "In a few days, it will be the anniversary of the sorrow that never leaves me, that will never leave me for the rest of my life."[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997526-145) She told another friend in 1971, "I suppose I suffer from very deep [depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(mood) "Depression (mood)")."[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994506-146) One biographer claims that she could have been [bipolar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipolar_disorder "Bipolar disorder"). "I am very happy one moment, the next there is nothing left for me", she said in 1933.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994506-146)

Beginning in the 1940s, Garbo became an art collector. Although many of the paintings she owned were of negligible monetary value, she also owned valuable works by [Renoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Auguste_Renoir "Pierre-Auguste Renoir"), [Rouault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Rouault "Georges Rouault"), [Kandinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassily_Kandinsky "Wassily Kandinsky"), [Bonnard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bonnard "Pierre Bonnard")[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997426%E2%80%93427,_530-147) and [Jawlensky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexej_von_Jawlensky "Alexej von Jawlensky").[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBroman1990227-148) Her art collection was worth millions of dollars when she died in 1990.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994344-149)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Greta_Garbo_in_1950.jpg/250px-Greta_Garbo_in_1950.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta_Garbo_in_1950.jpg)

Garbo signing her US citizenship papers in February 1951

On 9 February 1951, she became a [naturalized citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalized_citizen "Naturalized citizen") of the United States,[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-WhoLLC1983-150)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:1-3) and in 1953 bought a seven-room apartment at 450 East 52nd Street in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"),[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Kalins_Wise1968-151) where she lived for the rest of her life.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-WhoLLC1983-150) Her New York apartment buzzer was identified by a solitary G and the interior was a "light and airy study in pink".[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:2-140) In order to protect her privacy, she preferred being addressed as "Miss [Harriet] Brown".[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:3-135) Her close friends were only allowed to call her Miss Garbo or G.G.; if they called her Greta, she wouldn't respond.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-152)

Garbo was a dinner guest at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") on 13 November 1963, just nine days before the [assassination of JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_President_Kennedy "Assassination of President Kennedy").[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Pitts_2007_205%E2%80%93206-153) She spent the night at the Washington, D.C. home of philanthropist[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-latimes/me-mahoney21-154) Florence Stephenson Mahoney.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994468%E2%80%93469-155)[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997519%E2%80%93520-156) Garbo's niece reported that Garbo had always spoken of it as a "magical evening".[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-157)

Italian film director [Luchino Visconti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luchino_Visconti "Luchino Visconti") allegedly attempted to bring Garbo back to the screen in 1969 with the small part of [Maria Sophia, Queen of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Sophie_of_Bavaria "Maria Sophie of Bavaria") in his adaptation of [Proust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Proust "Marcel Proust")'s _[Remembrance of Things Past](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Search\_of\_Lost\_Time "In Search of Lost Time")_. He exclaimed: "I am very pleased with the idea that this woman, with her severe and authoritarian presence, should figure in the decadent and rarefied climate of the world described by Proust."[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994460-158) Claims that Garbo was interested in the part cannot be substantiated.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997541-159)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994460-158)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Greta-Garbo-1961.jpg/250px-Greta-Garbo-1961.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta-Garbo-1961.jpg)

Garbo in Stockholm in 1961

In 1971, Garbo vacationed in Southern France at the summer home of her close friend Baroness Cécile [de Rothschild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Rothschild "De Rothschild")[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickers2002-160) who introduced her to [Samuel Adams Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Adams_Green "Samuel Adams Green"), an art collector and curator in New York City.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-TelgObit-161) Green became an important friend and walking companion. He was in the habit of tape-recording all of his telephone calls, including many of his conversations with Garbo. He did so with her permission, but Garbo ended the friendship in 1981 after being falsely told that Green had played the tapes to friends.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994526-162) In his last will and testament, Green bequeathed all of the tapes in 2011 to the film archives at [Wesleyan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_University "Wesleyan University").[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-WaStars-163) The tapes reveal Garbo's personality in later life, her sense of humor, and various eccentricities. In 1977, Garbo wrote to Frederick Sands: "I am forever running away from something or somebody"... "Unconsciously I have always known that I was not destined for real and lasting happiness."[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:2-140)

Although she was increasingly withdrawn in her final years,[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994506%E2%80%93511-164) Garbo became close to her cook and housekeeper Claire Koger, who worked for her for 31 years. "We were very close—like sisters," Koger said.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994537%E2%80%93538-165)

Throughout her life, Garbo was known for taking long daily walks with companions or by herself. In retirement, she walked the streets of New York City, dressed casually and wearing large sunglasses. "Garbo-watching" became a sport for photographers, the media, admirers, and curious New Yorkers,[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994495%E2%80%93505-166) but she strictly maintained her privacy and her elusive mystique followed her to the end.

[Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegians "Norwegians") actress [Liv Ullmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liv_Ullmann "Liv Ullmann"), who was dubbed "The New Greta Garbo",[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-167) and played [Anna Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Christie "Anna Christie") on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") in 1977,[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-168) saw Garbo in the street and ran after her, in hopes of meeting her and telling her she was playing Anna Christie. Garbo ran away from her and disappeared into [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park"). Ullmann gave up the chase after she saw that Garbo looked "frightened". She said: "Yes, she outpaced me. But when she turned and looked so frightened I gave up and didn't follow her. I was younger; I could have made it, but I didn't."[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-169)

### Relationships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Greta_Garbo&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Relationships")]

Garbo never married, had no children, and lived alone for most of her adult life. She once said: "If I were ever to love anyone, it would be [Mauritz Stiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritz_Stiller "Mauritz Stiller")."[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-170)

Her most famous romance was with her frequent MGM co-star [John Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gilbert_(actor) "John Gilbert (actor)"), with whom she lived intermittently in 1926 and 1927.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997122%E2%80%93127,_129%E2%80%93135-171) Soon after their romance began, Gilbert began helping her develop acting skills on the set and teaching her how to behave like a star, socialize at parties, and deal with studio bosses.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Gross-172) They co-starred again in three more hits: _Love_ (1927), _[A Woman of Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Woman\_of\_Affairs "A Woman of Affairs")_ (1928), and _[Queen Christina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen\_Christina\_(film) "Queen Christina (film)")_ (1933). Gilbert allegedly proposed to Garbo numerous times and she finally accepted, but backed out just before the wedding.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Gross-172)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira200538-4)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994125-173) "I was in love with him," she said. "But I froze. I was afraid he would tell me what to do and boss me. I always wanted to be the boss." In later years when asked about Gilbert, Garbo said "I can't remember what I ever saw in him."[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Gross-172) According to [Ava Gardner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ava_Gardner "Ava Gardner")'s autobiography, Garbo admitted to her that Gilbert was the only man she'd ever really loved but he had "let [her] down" by having a "superstitious affair" with "a little extra" during their last film and she had never forgiven him.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-174)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Greta_Garbo_1946_by_Cecil_Beaton.jpg/250px-Greta_Garbo_1946_by_Cecil_Beaton.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Greta_Garbo_1946_by_Cecil_Beaton.jpg)

Garbo photographed by [Cecil Beaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Beaton "Cecil Beaton"), 1946

In 1937, Garbo met [Leopold Stokowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Stokowski "Leopold Stokowski"), then conductor of the [Philadelphia Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Orchestra "Philadelphia Orchestra"), with whom she had a brief, but highly publicized relationship while the pair traveled throughout Europe the following year; whether the relationship was romantic or platonic is uncertain.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997368%E2%80%93382-175)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994349%E2%80%93351,_353%E2%80%93355-176) In his diary, German novelist [Erich Maria Remarque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Maria_Remarque "Erich Maria Remarque") discusses a liaison with Garbo in 1941,[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997414%E2%80%93415-177) and in his memoir, British photographer [Cecil Beaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Beaton "Cecil Beaton") described an affair with her in 1947 and 1948.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997457%E2%80%93460-178)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994404%E2%80%93409-179) They maintained a romantic friendship for several years, during which Beaton hoped to marry her, though his feelings were often unreciprocated as he competed with George Schlee for her affection.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-180)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-181)[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:6-182) He later reflected, "Greta was a full-time job and an anxiety as well as a pleasure."[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-:6-182)

In 1941, Garbo met the Russian-born millionaire George Schlee, who was introduced to her by his wife, fashion designer [Valentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentina_(fashion_designer) "Valentina (fashion designer)"). Nicholas Turner, Garbo's close friend for 33 years, said that, after she bought an apartment in the same building, "Garbo moved in and took Schlee from Valentina right away."[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-Gross-172) Schlee would divide his time between the two, becoming Garbo's close companion and advisor until his death in 1964.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997428%E2%80%93504-183)[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994412%E2%80%93552-184)

Recent biographers and others have speculated that, because it can be assumed she had intimate relationships with women as well as men, Garbo was [bisexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisexuality "Bisexuality"), possibly even "predominantly [lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian")".[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-191) In 1927, Garbo was introduced to stage and screen actress [Lilyan Tashman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilyan_Tashman "Lilyan Tashman"), and they may have had an affair, according to some writers.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994251%E2%80%93255-192)[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVieira200526-193) Silent film star [Louise Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Brooks "Louise Brooks") stated that she and Garbo had a brief liaison the following year.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-194)

In 1931, Garbo befriended the writer and acknowledged lesbian [Mercedes de Acosta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_de_Acosta "Mercedes de Acosta"), whom she met through [Salka Viertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salka_Viertel "Salka Viertel"), and, according to Garbo's and de Acosta's biographers, began a sporadic and volatile romance.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchanke2003-195)[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-196) The two remained friends—with ups and downs—for almost 30 years, during which time Garbo wrote de Acosta 181 letters, cards, and telegrams, now at the [Rosenbach Museum and Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosenbach_Museum_and_Library "Rosenbach Museum and Library") in Philadelphia.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997381,_511-197)[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParis1994264-198) Garbo's family, which controls her estate,[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwenson1997559-199) has made only 87 of these items publicly available.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo#cite_note-200)
