[Lord Snowdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Snowdon "Lord Snowdon").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-33) The film reached No. 1 in the UK box-office charts in April that year, a position it held for five consecutive weeks.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Swern-1995-28)

Jackson made the first of several appearances with [Morecambe and Wise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morecambe_and_Wise "Morecambe and Wise") in their 1971 Christmas special. Appearing in a comedy sketch as [Cleopatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleopatra "Cleopatra") for the BBC _[Morecambe and Wise Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Morecambe\_&\_Wise\_Show\_(1968%E2%80%931977) "The Morecambe & Wise Show (1968–1977)")_, she delivered the line, "All men are fools and what makes them so is having beauty like what I have got."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-34) Her later appearances included a song-and-dance routine (where she was pushed offstage by Eric), a period drama about [Queen Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria"), and another musical routine (in their [Thames Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Television "Thames Television") series) where she was elevated ten feet in the air by a misbehaving swivel chair.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-36) Jackson and Wise also appeared in a 1981 information film for the [Blood Transfusion Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_Transfusion_Service "Blood Transfusion Service").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-37)

Filmmaker [Melvin Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Frank "Melvin Frank") saw Jackson's comedy skills in the _Morecambe and Wise Show_ and offered her the lead female role in his romantic comedy _[A Touch of Class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Touch\_of\_Class\_(film) "A Touch of Class (film)")_ (1973), co-starring [George Segal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Segal "George Segal"), which was a UK box-office No. 1 in June 1973.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Swern-1995-28) In February 1974, Jackson's role in the film won her the Academy Award for Best Actress. She continued to work in the theatre, returning to the RSC for the lead in [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen")'s _[Hedda Gabler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedda\_Gabler "Hedda Gabler")_. A later film version directed by [Trevor Nunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Nunn "Trevor Nunn") was released as _[Hedda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedda\_(1975\_film) "Hedda (1975 film)")_ (1975), for which Jackson was nominated for an Oscar. In _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, [Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby") wrote: "This version of _Hedda Gabler_ is all Miss Jackson's Hedda and, I must say, great fun to watch ... Miss Jackson's technical virtuosity is particularly suited to a character like Hedda. Her command of her voice and her body, as well as the Jackson mannerisms, have the effect of separating the actress from the character in a very curious way."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-38)

In 1978, she starred in the romantic comedy _[House Calls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_Calls\_(1978\_film) "House Calls (1978 film)"),_ co-starring [Walter Matthau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Matthau "Walter Matthau"), with the film spending two weeks at No. 1 in the US box-office rankings.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-41)_House Calls_ was the biggest box-office hit of her career in the United States.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-42) That year, she was awarded a [CBE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBE "CBE").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-WHO'S_WHO_&_WHO_WAS_WHO-2007-10) In 1979, she reunited with her _A Touch of Class_ colleagues Segal and Frank for the romantic comedy _[Lost and Found](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost\_and\_Found\_(1979\_film) "Lost and Found (1979 film)")_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-44) Jackson and Matthau teamed again in the comedy _[Hopscotch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopscotch\_(film) "Hopscotch (film)")_ (1980), which debuted at No. 1 in its opening weekend at the US box office, also spending its second week in the top spot.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-47)

### 1980–1991: Established actor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Glenda_Jackson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1980–1991: Established actor")]

For her 1980 appearance on _[The Muppet Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Muppet\_Show "The Muppet Show")_, Jackson told the producers she would perform any material they liked. In her appearance, she has a delusion that she is a pirate captain who takes over the Muppet Theatre as her ship.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-48) Fifteen years after the New York engagement of _[Marat/Sade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marat/Sade "Marat/Sade")_, Jackson returned to Broadway in [Andrew Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Davies_(writer) "Andrew Davies (writer)")'s _Rose_ (1981) opposite [Jessica Tandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Tandy "Jessica Tandy"); both actresses received Tony nominations for their roles.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-49) In September 1983, The Glenda Jackson Theatre in Birkenhead was named in her honour. The theatre was attached to [Wirral Metropolitan College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wirral_Metropolitan_College "Wirral Metropolitan College"), but demolished in 2005 following the establishment of a purpose-built site for students.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-50)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Amerikaanse_tv-show_Laat_Polen_Polen_zijn_op_de_televisie._Glenda_Jackson_tijd%2C_Bestanddeelnr_931-9473.jpg/250px-Amerikaanse_tv-show_Laat_Polen_Polen_zijn_op_de_televisie._Glenda_Jackson_tijd%2C_Bestanddeelnr_931-9473.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amerikaanse_tv-show_Laat_Polen_Polen_zijn_op_de_televisie._Glenda_Jackson_tijd,_Bestanddeelnr_931-9473.jpg)

Jackson on _[Let Poland be Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let\_Poland\_be\_Poland\_(TV) "Let Poland be Poland (TV)")_ (1982)

In 1985, she played Nina Leeds in a revival of [Eugene O'Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_O'Neill "Eugene O'Neill")'s _[Strange Interlude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Interlude "Strange Interlude")_ at the [Nederlander Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nederlander_Theatre "Nederlander Theatre") in a production which had originated in London the previous year and ran for eight weeks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Chambers-9) John Beaufort for _[The Christian Science Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Christian\_Science\_Monitor "The Christian Science Monitor")_ wrote: "Bravura is the inevitable word for Miss Jackson's display of feminine wiles and brilliant technique."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-51)[Frank Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Rich "Frank Rich") in _The New York Times_ thought Jackson, "with her helmet of hair and gashed features", when Leeds is a young woman, "looks like a cubist portrait of [Louise Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Brooks "Louise Brooks")", and later when the character has aged several decades, is "mesmerizing as a [Zelda Fitzgeraldesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zelda_Fitzgerald "Zelda Fitzgerald") neurotic, a rotting and spiteful middle-aged matron and, finally, a spent, [sphinx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphinx "Sphinx")-like widow happily embracing extinction."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-52)[Herbert Wise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Wise "Herbert Wise") directed the drama on television where it was first broadcast in the US as part of PBS's _[American Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Playhouse "American Playhouse")_ in 1988.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-53)

In November 1984, Jackson appeared in the title role of [Robert David MacDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_David_MacDonald "Robert David MacDonald")'s English translation of [Racine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Racine "Jean Racine")'s _[Phèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph%C3%A8dre "Phèdre")_, titled _Phedra_, at [The Old Vic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Old_Vic "The Old Vic"). The play was designed and directed by [Philip Prowse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Prowse "Philip Prowse"), and [Robert Eddison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Eddison "Robert Eddison") played [Theramenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theramenes "Theramenes").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-55)_[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_'s John Barber wrote of her performance, "Wonderfully impressive ... The actress finds a voice as jagged and hoarse as her torment". [Benedict Nightingale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_Nightingale "Benedict Nightingale") in the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_ was intrigued that Jackson did not go in for nobility, but played Racine's feverish queen as if to say that "being skewered in the guts by [Cupid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupid "Cupid") is an ugly, bitter, humiliating business".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-56) The costume which Prowse designed for Jackson's performance is in the [Victoria and Albert Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_and_Albert_Museum "Victoria and Albert Museum"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-57) and iconic photographs of Jackson in the role can be found online.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-59)

In 1989, Jackson appeared in Ken Russell's _[The Rainbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rainbow\_(1989\_film) "The Rainbow (1989 film)")_, playing Anna Brangwen, mother of Gudrun, the part for which she had won her first Academy Award twenty years earlier. The same year, she played Martha in a Los Angeles production of [Edward Albee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Albee "Edward Albee")'s _[Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who's\_Afraid\_of\_Virginia\_Woolf%3F "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?")_ at the Doolittle Theatre (now the [Ricardo Montalbán Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Montalb%C3%A1n_Theatre "Ricardo Montalbán Theatre")). Directed by the playwright himself, this staging featured [John Lithgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lithgow "John Lithgow") as George. [Dan Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Sullivan_(critic) "Dan Sullivan (critic)") in the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ wrote that Jackson and Lithgow performed "with the assurance of dedicated character assassins, not your hire-and-salary types" with the actors being able to display their character's capacity for antipathy.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-60) Albee was disappointed with this production, pointing to Jackson, who he thought "had retreated back to the thing she can do very well, that ice cold performance. I don't know whether she got scared, but in rehearsal she was being Martha, and the closer we got to opening the less Martha she was!"[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-61) She performed the lead role in [Howard Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Barker "Howard Barker")'s _[Scenes from an Execution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scenes\_from\_an\_Execution "Scenes from an Execution")_ as Galactia, a sixteenth-century female [Venetian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice") artist, at the [Almeida Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Theatre "Almeida Theatre") in 1990.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-62) It was an adaptation of Barker's 1984 radio play in which Jackson had played the same role.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-63)

### 2015–2023: Return to acting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Glenda_Jackson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2015–2023: Return to acting")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/GlendaJackBFI050722_%2810_of_23%29_%2852196800013%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-GlendaJackBFI050722_%2810_of_23%29_%2852196800013%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GlendaJackBFI050722_(10_of_23)_(52196800013)_(cropped).jpg)

Jackson at BFI London in 2022

In 2015, Jackson returned to acting following a 23-year absence, having retired from politics. She took the lead role of Dide, the ancient matriarch, in _Blood, Sex and Money_, a [radio drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_drama "Radio drama") series based on the _[Les Rougon-Macquart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_Rougon-Macquart "Les Rougon-Macquart")_ novel series by [Émile Zola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Zola "Émile Zola") and aired on [Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4") from November 2015 to October 2016.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-spectator-20151203-64) She returned to the stage at the end of 2016, playing the title role in [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare")'s _[King Lear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King\_Lear "King Lear")_ at the [Old Vic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Vic "Old Vic") Theatre in London, in a production running from 25 October to 3 December. Jackson was nominated for Best Actress at the [Olivier Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_Awards "Olivier Awards") for her performance but ultimately lost out to [Billie Piper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Piper "Billie Piper"). She won the [Natasha Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natasha_Richardson "Natasha Richardson") Award for Best Actress at the 2017 [Evening Standard Theatre Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_Theatre_Awards "Evening Standard Theatre Awards") for her performance.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-lear-65) Dominic Cavendish of _[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ wrote, "Glenda Jackson is tremendous as King Lear. No ifs, no buts. In returning to the stage at the age of 80, 25 years after her last performance (as the [Clytemnestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clytemnestra "Clytemnestra")-like Christine in [Eugene O'Neill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_O'Neill "Eugene O'Neill")'s _[Mourning Becomes Electra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourning\_Becomes\_Electra "Mourning Becomes Electra")_ at the [Glasgow Citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizens_Theatre "Citizens Theatre")), she has pulled off one of those 11th-hour feats of human endeavour that will surely be talked about for years to come by those who see it."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-66)

In 2018, Jackson returned to [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(theatre) "Broadway (theatre)") in a revival of [Edward Albee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Albee "Edward Albee")'s _[Three Tall Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three\_Tall\_Women "Three Tall Women")_ acting alongside [Laurie Metcalf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurie_Metcalf "Laurie Metcalf") and [Allison Pill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allison_Pill "Allison Pill").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-67) The role earned her the [Tony Award for Best Actress in a Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Award_for_Best_Actress_in_a_Play "Tony Award for Best Actress in a Play").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-68)[Marilyn Stasio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_Stasio "Marilyn Stasio") of _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ wrote, "Watching Glenda Jackson in theatrical flight is like looking straight into the sun. Her expressive face registers her thoughts while guarding her feelings. But it's the voice that really thrills. Deeply pitched and clarion clear, it's the commanding voice of stern authority. Don't mess with this household god or she'll turn you to stone."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-69) Jackson returned to the title role of _[King Lear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King\_Lear "King Lear")_ on Broadway in a production that opened in April 2019.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-70) Director [Sam Gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Gold "Sam Gold") described her portrayal of Lear in _[The New York Times Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Magazine "The New York Times Magazine")_: "She is going to go through something most people don't go through. You're all invited. Glenda Jackson is going to endure this, and you're going to witness it."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-71) In 2019, after a 27-year absence, Jackson returned to television drama, portraying an elderly grandmother struggling with dementia in _[Elizabeth Is Missing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth\_Is\_Missing "Elizabeth Is Missing")_ on [BBC One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_One "BBC One"), based on the novel of the same name by [Emma Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Healey "Emma Healey"), for which she won the [BAFTA TV Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Television_Award_for_Best_Actress "British Academy Television Award for Best Actress") and [International Emmy Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Emmy_Award_for_Best_Actress "International Emmy Award for Best Actress").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-73) From February 2020 to January 2022, she starred in the lead role of Constance Sterling in the radio drama series _Fault Lines: Money, Sex and Blood_ for Radio 4, another adaptation of _Les Rougon-Macquart_.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-74)

In February 2021, it was reported that Jackson would star with [Michael Caine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine") in _[The Great Escaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Great\_Escaper "The Great Escaper")_, a film telling the true story of [Bernard Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Jordan "Bernard Jordan")'s escape from his care home to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the [D-Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-Day "D-Day") landings in France. Caine would play Jordan, with Jackson as his wife Rene.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-75) Caine and Jackson previously starred together in _[The Romantic Englishwoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Romantic\_Englishwoman "The Romantic Englishwoman")_ (1975).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-76) Jackson had completed filming on _The Great Escaper_ in September 2022; it was to be her last film.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-iNews33-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Guardian33-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Pathe33-79) It was released on 6 October 2023.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-BBC_News-2023-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-81) In July 2022, the [British Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film Institute") celebrated her film and television career with a month-long retrospective season at the [BFI Southbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BFI_Southbank "BFI Southbank") in London. As well as screenings of her work, the programme included _Glenda Jackson in Conversation_, in which she was interviewed about her career live on stage by broadcaster [John Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilson_(broadcaster) "John Wilson (broadcaster)").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Griffiths-2022-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-84)

## Political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Glenda_Jackson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Political career")]

Jackson joined the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") in the early 1950s, at the age of 16.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-85) Her earlier campaigns were not party political. In 1978, she was one of the public figures who lent their name as a sponsor to the [Anti-Nazi League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Nazi_League "Anti-Nazi League").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-86) The same year, she appeared in a print advertisement for [Oxfam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxfam "Oxfam").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-87) Jackson was on the executive of the National Association of Voluntary Hostels, and spoke at rallies for the housing charity [Shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelter_(charity) "Shelter (charity)"). Human rights were also an area of interest, and she joined a demonstration outside the Indonesian Embassy to protest against the detention of political prisoners. She was involved in children's charities, as president of the Toy Libraries Association and as a programme narrator for [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF"). She also gave time and money to a home for emotionally disturbed children in [Berkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire "Berkshire") run by former actress [Coral Atkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Atkins "Coral Atkins").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Bryant-1999-88)

Jackson was a supporter of the [National Abortion Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Abortion_Campaign "National Abortion Campaign"), and organised a benefit evening for them at the [Cambridge Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Theatre "Cambridge Theatre"), which raised over £3,000. She also supported [Una Kroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Una_Kroll "Una Kroll")'s Women's Rights candidacy for [Sutton and Cheam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_and_Cheam "Sutton and Cheam") in the [October 1974 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_1974_United_Kingdom_general_election "October 1974 United Kingdom general election"). In addition, Jackson made several appearances on [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4")'s _[Any Questions?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Any\_Questions%3F "Any Questions?")_ debate programme during this period of her career.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Bryant-1999-88) She had considered becoming a social worker, and in 1979 began a social science degree at the [Open University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_University "Open University"), but dropped out a few months later after falling behind with her essays.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Bryant-1999-3-89) Jackson appeared in a number of charity films, including a production on behalf of [International Year of the Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Year_of_the_Child "International Year of the Child"), [Voluntary Service Overseas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voluntary_Service_Overseas "Voluntary Service Overseas"), and Oxfam. Other such films featured her campaigning against [polio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio "Polio") and the arms trade.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-90)

### Labour Party

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Glenda_Jackson&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Labour Party")]

Jackson's name was linked to several parliamentary seats over the years; she was approached by a [Constituency Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituency_Labour_Party "Constituency Labour Party") (CLP) in Bristol to stand at the [1979 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_United_Kingdom_general_election "1979 United Kingdom general election"), but this did not materialise.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Bryant-1999-88)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-92) An approach was also made to her about the possibility of being a candidate for the [marginal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_seat "Marginal seat") Welsh seat of [Bridgend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgend_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Bridgend (UK Parliament constituency)") at the [1983 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_United_Kingdom_general_election "1983 United Kingdom general election"), which she turned down to pursue a humanities degree at [Thames Polytechnic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Polytechnic "Thames Polytechnic"). Though she was seen in the refectory at Thames a few times, she dropped out before starting the course.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Bryant-1999-3-89) In that election, she supported [Paul Boateng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Boateng "Paul Boateng") and Ian Wilson, Labour's candidates for [Hertfordshire West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertfordshire_West "Hertfordshire West") and [Watford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watford_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Watford (UK Parliament constituency)"), respectively. She was also a member of the Arts for Labour group.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Woodward-1985-91)

In 1986, Jackson visited Ethiopia as part of Oxfam's efforts to help with [the famine there](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983%E2%80%931985_famine_in_Ethiopia "1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia"), and in 1989 she approached [Voluntary Service Overseas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voluntary_Service_Overseas "Voluntary Service Overseas") about the chance of working in Africa for a couple of years. She got involved in the [African National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_National_Congress "African National Congress") campaign against [apartheid in South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid_in_South_Africa "Apartheid in South Africa"), and in September 1988 chaired a United Nations committee on the cultural boycott.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Bryant-1999-3-89) Jackson appeared in a [party political broadcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_political_broadcast "Party political broadcast") for Labour in February 1987.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-93) In June, she was present at a campaign rally with the then Labour leader [Neil Kinnock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Kinnock "Neil Kinnock") for the [1987 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_United_Kingdom_general_election "1987 United Kingdom general election").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-94)

In December 1989, it was rumoured that Jackson had been approached by two branches of [Leeds East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_East "Leeds East") CLP to succeed their Labour MP, [Denis Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Healey "Denis Healey"). According to her biographer [Chris Bryant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bryant "Chris Bryant"), she turned down this opportunity. In late 1989, two members of [Hampstead and Highgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_and_Highgate "Hampstead and Highgate") CLP got in touch with Jackson about the possibility of standing there. Despite having never been to a Labour ward meeting, she won over the local party, and triumphed in the ballot, which took place on 28 March 1990. Jackson defeated three candidates who were all politically to her left: [Kate Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Allen_(Amnesty_International) "Kate Allen (Amnesty International)") ([Ken Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Livingstone "Ken Livingstone")'s partner and a [Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_London_Borough_Council "Camden London Borough Council") councillor), economic history lecturer Sarah Palmer (daughter of former Labour MP [Arthur Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Palmer_(politician) "Arthur Palmer (politician)")) and Maureen Robinson, a previous Mayor of Camden.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-95)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-97)

Jackson later stated that she felt Britain was being "destroyed" by the policies of the then [prime minister of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime minister of the United Kingdom"), [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher"), and the Conservative government, so that she was willing to do "anything that was legal" to oppose them.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-98) In November 1990, Thatcher stood down as prime minister and [leader of the Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Conservative_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Conservative Party (UK)"). On Thatcher's death, Jackson protested Parliament's tributes to that legacy.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-99)

### In Parliament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Glenda_Jackson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In Parliament")]

Jackson retired from acting in 1991 to devote herself to politics full-time as the [prospective parliamentary candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospective_parliamentary_candidate "Prospective parliamentary candidate") for Hampstead and Highgate.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-100) Although her party did not win the [1992 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_Kingdom_general_election "1992 United Kingdom general election"), as had been speculated, there was an above average swing to Labour in her constituency, and she gained the seat, narrowly beating the Conservative candidate [Oliver Letwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Letwin "Oliver Letwin"), a former adviser to Thatcher.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-103) Jackson, whose campaign had been sponsored by the train drivers' union, [ASLEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASLEF "ASLEF"), was the first of Labour's 1992 intake to join the front bench when she became shadow transport minister in July 1996.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-105)

Following Labour's [landslide victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide_victory "Landslide victory") in the [1997 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election "1997 United Kingdom general election"), which saw her comfortably re-elected, she was appointed as a junior minister in the government of [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair"),[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-Debretts-106) with responsibility in the [London Regional Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Regional_Transport "London Regional Transport").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-electionhub.co.uk-107) She resigned from the post in 1999 before an unsuccessful attempt to be nominated as the Labour candidate for the election of the first [mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London "Mayor of London") in the [2000 London mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_London_mayoral_election "2000 London mayoral election"). In the [2000 London Labour Party mayoral selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_London_Labour_Party_mayoral_selection "2000 London Labour Party mayoral selection"), she came a distant third behind [Frank Dobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson "Frank Dobson") and [Ken Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Livingstone "Ken Livingstone"), being eliminated in the first round of voting with 4.4% of the total.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-108) Jackson was once again re-elected to represent her constituency at the [2001 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_United_Kingdom_general_election "2001 United Kingdom general election").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-109)

As a high-profile backbencher, Jackson became a regular critic of Blair over his plans to introduce [higher education tuition fees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuition_fees_in_the_United_Kingdom "Tuition fees in the United Kingdom") in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland. She also called for him to resign following the Judicial Enquiry by [Lord Hutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Hutton,_Baron_Hutton "Brian Hutton, Baron Hutton") in 2003 surrounding the reasons for going to [war in Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") and the death of government adviser [David Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Kelly_(weapons_expert) "David Kelly (weapons expert)").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-The_Guardian-2020-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-113) At the subsequent [2005 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_United_Kingdom_general_election "2005 United Kingdom general election"), she held her seat, albeit with a reduced majority and a swing to the Conservatives, who had selected local councillor [Piers Wauchope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piers_Wauchope "Piers Wauchope").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-114) By October 2005, her disagreements with Blair's leadership swelled to a point where she threatened to challenge the prime minister as a [stalking horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalking_horse "Stalking horse") candidate in a leadership contest if he did not stand down within a reasonable amount of time.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-115) On 31 October 2006, Jackson was one of 12 Labour MPs to back [Plaid Cymru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaid_Cymru "Plaid Cymru") and the [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party")'s call for an inquiry into the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-116)

Her constituency boundaries changed for the [2010 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election "2010 United Kingdom general election"). The [Gospel Oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_Oak_(ward) "Gospel Oak (ward)") and [Highgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highgate_(Camden_ward) "Highgate (Camden ward)") wards became part of [Holborn and St Pancras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holborn_and_St_Pancras "Holborn and St Pancras"), and the new [Hampstead and Kilburn constituency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_and_Kilburn_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Hampstead and Kilburn (UK Parliament constituency)") took in territory from [Brent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Brent "London Borough of Brent") to include Brondesbury, Kilburn and Queens Park wards (from the old [Brent East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brent_East "Brent East") and [Brent South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brent_South "Brent South") seats). On 6 May 2010, Jackson was elected as the MP for the new Hampstead and Kilburn constituency by a margin of 42 votes over Conservative [Chris Philp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Philp "Chris Philp"), with the [Liberal Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") candidate Edward Fordham less than a thousand votes behind them. She had the closest result in England, and the second smallest majority of any MP at the 2010 election.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-117)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-119) Jackson's seat was marginal for most of her time in politics, with the 1997 election being the only occasion on which she received an absolute majority of votes cast in the constituency.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-electionhub.co.uk-107)

In June 2011, Jackson announced that, presuming the [UK Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Parliament "UK Parliament") elected in 2010 lasted until 2015, she would not seek re-election. She stated: "I will be almost 80 and by then it will be time for someone else to have a turn."[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-reelection-120) The eventual election was held two days before her 79th birthday, 23 years after she had first entered the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom"). In April 2012, the _[London Evening Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London\_Evening\_Standard "London Evening Standard")_ reported that, in 2007–2008 she claimed £136,793 in allowances despite turning up for only 27 per cent of votes and speaking in just two debates, and that in 2011 she had to repay more than £8,000 in expenses she had wrongly claimed.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-121)

On 10 April 2013, Jackson delivered a speech in the House of Commons following the [death of Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_Margaret_Thatcher "Death of Margaret Thatcher"), which subsequently went viral.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-122) She accused [Thatcherism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thatcherism "Thatcherism") of treating "vices as virtues" and stated that, because of Thatcherism, the UK was susceptible to unprecedented unemployment rates and homelessness, chronically underfunded schools and public services, and the closure of mental hospitals.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-123)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-124) Another speech of Jackson's went viral in June 2014 when she gave a scathing assessment of [Iain Duncan Smith's tenure as Work and Pensions Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Duncan_Smith's_tenure_as_Work_and_Pensions_Secretary "Iain Duncan Smith's tenure as Work and Pensions Secretary"), telling him that he was responsible for the "destruction of the welfare state and the total and utter incompetence of his department".[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenda_Jackson#cite_note-126)

### Views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Glenda_Jackson&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Views")]

Jackson was a borderline [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist "Socialist"), and was generally considered to be a traditional [leftist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leftist "Leftist") during her political career, often disagreeing with the dominant [Blairite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blairite "Blairite") governing [Third Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Way "Third Way") faction in the Labour Party; she rebelled against her party in parliamentary votes on a number of occasions. She was also opposed to the politics of [Arthur Scargill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Scargill "Arthur Scargill") and the [Militant tendency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militant_tendency "Militant tendency") that dominated the party's battles in the 1980s.
